Unit 2 - Project Management: How to set up a Research Project

James Flynn

August 31, 2026

Writing a research paper is a massive undertaking

  • Come up with idea
  • Read relevant literature
  • Find appropriate data source to answer question
  • Perform analysis
  • Test results (robustness)
  • Write paper
  • Edit paper
  • Present paper
  • Submit paper (desk-reject)
  • Submit paper (reject with reviews)
  • Submit paper (R&R!!!)

Still not done…

What happends when you submit a paper?

  • First, your paper goes to the editor
  • They read it and decide:
    • Desk-reject the paper (usually happens quick)
    • Send to referees

It went to referees! What now…

  • Usually at least two (I’ve had up to five)
  • Each referee will read the paper and:
    • Write a referee report
    • Make a recommendation (reject, R&R)
  • Editor then makes a decision
    • Reject
    • Revise and Resubmit (R&R)
    • Occasionally, reject and resubmit

If you get an R&R

  • Celebrate!!!
  • But then there is work to do
  • Average top-five pub has three rounds of revision
  • Mean T5 submit-to-accept time is 26 months!*
  • Much shorter at field journals, but still takes a while

*Hadavand et al (2021)

The point is, organization is crucial

  • Many journals require replication packages
  • Need to keep track of
    • Raw data
    • Cleaned data
    • Code
    • Graphs
    • Tables
    • Drafts of paper
  • This is all true for public/private sector as well

Best way to keep track is with a project folder

Then we can create sub-folders

Project Management Tips

1: comment, Comment, COMMENT your code

#this line creates a normal random variable
x <- rnorm(1000)
#this line creates a uniform random variable
y <- runif(1000)
#this line gives a scatterplot of x and y
plot(x,y)

2 - Indent your code when it goes for multiple lines

  • This will be especially common in tidyverse
#load mort_2021 data
load("mort_21.RData")

#create new variable for women
mort_2021 <- mort_2021 %>%
  mutate(female = ifelse(sex == "F", 1, 0))

2 - Indent your code (cont’d)

  • Otherwise it can look like this:
mort_2021 %>% mutate(female = ifelse(sex == "F", 1, 0),
married = marstat == "M", autopsy_performed = autopsy == "Y",
years_ed = as.numeric(ifelse(educ2003==1,8, ifelse(educ2003==2,10,
ifelse(educ2003==3,12, ifelse(educ2003==4,13, ifelse(educ2003==5,14,
ifelse(educ2003==6,16, ifelse(educ2003==7,18, ifelse(educ2003==8,21,NA))))))))),
age_years = as.numeric(ifelse(age==1999,NA, ifelse(age<2000,age-1000,0))),) %>%
filter(years_ed!="NA") %>% group_by(female) %>%  summarise(mean_ed = mean(years_ed), mean_age = mean(age))
## # A tibble: 2 × 3
##   female mean_ed mean_age
##    <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1      0    12.7    1084.
## 2      1    12.5    1089.

2 - Compare that to this

mort_2021 %>%
  mutate(female = ifelse(sex == "F", 1, 0),
         married = marstat == "M", 
         autopsy_performed = autopsy == "Y",
         years_ed = as.numeric(ifelse(educ2003==1,8, 
                               ifelse(educ2003==2,10,
                               ifelse(educ2003==3,12,
                               ifelse(educ2003==4,13,
                               ifelse(educ2003==5,14,
                               ifelse(educ2003==6,16,
                               ifelse(educ2003==7,18, 
                               ifelse(educ2003==8,21,NA))))))))),
         age_years = as.numeric(ifelse(age==1999,NA,
                                ifelse(age<2000,age-1000,0))),) %>%
  filter(years_ed!="NA") %>% 
  group_by(female) %>%  
  summarise(mean_ed = mean(years_ed), mean_age = mean(age_years))
## # A tibble: 2 × 3
##   female mean_ed mean_age
##    <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1      0    12.7     69.3
## 2      1    12.5     75.4

3 - Aim for efficiency, but don’t become obsessed

  • Often times, you can take what you’ve done in 10 lines, and do it all in one or two
  • This is very helpful for someone reading your code
  • However, if your code gets the job done, don’t waste hours trying to improve it

4 - Use intuitive names for objects

  • Earlier slide:
    • mort_2021 was NVSS mortality data from 2021
    • female was a binary variable where 1 means the subject is female

5 - Keep separate parts of the project separate

  • Scripts
  • Data
  • Graphs
  • Tables
  • Drafts

Should each have their own folder

6 - Aim for cohesion across datasets

  • If two datasets have the same variable, make sure they have the same name
  • This will make it easier when it comes time to merge them

7 - Name scripts numerically

  • 01_data_clean.R
  • 02_make_graph.R
  • 03_run_regressions.R
  • 04_robustness_checks.R

(Replication packages will require this anyways)

Ok, let’s write a fake paper

  • We will be using some data I scraped from IMDB’s top 250 movies
  • We will look at whether movies which get more votes also receive higher ratings

Getting started

  • Installing and loading packages the old fashioned way
#install.packages("ggplot2")
#install.packages("tidyverse")
#install.packages("stargazer")
#install.packages("texreg")
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(stargazer)
library(texreg)

Installing and loading packages (CHEAT CODE)

packages = c("ggplot2","tidyverse","stargazer","texreg")

#this function checks if you have the necessary packages
#if you have them it loads them
#if you don't it installs and then loads them
package.check <- lapply(packages, FUN = function(x) {
  if (!require(x, character.only = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(x, dependencies = TRUE)
    library(x, character.only = TRUE)
  }
})

Other admin stuff

#This tells R where your data is
#setwd("C:/Users/flynn/OneDrive/Desktop/eco511_prjct")
#This clears everything out of your environment so you can start fresh
rm(list = ls())

#This gets rid of annoying scientific notation R defaults to in Graphs
options(scipen=999)

#This tells R to load an rds data file from your folder called "imdb250.rds"
imdb_data <- readRDS(file = "imdb250.rds")

Let’s look at our data

#This saves a scatter plot of votes received by year of film release
imdb_scatter <- ggplot(data = imdb_data, aes(x=year,y=votes/1000000)) +
                    geom_point() +
                    ylab("Millions of Votes") + 
                    xlab("Year of Release")
imdb_scatter

We can now export this graph to use in our paper

#This tells R to export this graph to my Graphs folder
#This first line tells R I want to save it as a png called imdb_scatter in Graphs
png("imdb_scatter.png")
#This tells R what graph I want to save
imdb_scatter
#This tells R that I am done and want it to execute the export
dev.off()
## png 
##   2

A little data cleaning

#Let's rescale the vote variable by 1,000,000
#and add a quadratic term for year
imdb_data <- imdb_data %>%
  mutate(mill_votes = votes/1000000,
         year_squared = year^2)

Running regressions!

lm1 <- lm(rating ~ mill_votes, data = imdb_data)
#summary(lm1)

lm2 <- lm(rating ~ mill_votes + year, data = imdb_data)
#summary(lm2)

lm3 <- lm(rating ~ mill_votes + year + year_squared, data = imdb_data)
#summary(lm3)

Exporting regression tables

  • First for Microsoft Word
#output table for Word
wordreg(list(lm1, lm2, lm3), stars = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05), 
        custom.coef.names = c("Intercept", "Millions of Votes", "Year", "Year Squared"),
        file = "Tables/imdb.doc")

Exporting regression tables

  • Now for latex
#output table for latex
stargazer(lm1, lm2, lm3, type = 'latex', 
          keep = c("mill_votes", "year", "year_squared"),
          covariate.labels=c("Millions of Votes","Year of Release", "Year Squared"), 
          dep.var.labels = c("Rating"),
          no.space=TRUE,
          keep.stat="n",
          out = "Tables/imdb.tex")

After looking at the regression table, do we need the quadratic?

imdb_quad <- ggplot(data = imdb_data, aes(y=rating,x=mill_votes)) +
                geom_point() +
                geom_smooth(method="lm") +
                geom_smooth(method="lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2)) +
                ylab("Rating") + 
                xlab("Millions of Votes")
imdb_quad
